title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] A lot of discussion has taken place about MathArena's evaluation on IMO 2025 and OpenAIs subsequent announcement of achieving the gold medal. A thread clarifying the most important arguments 🧵
────────
[2/4] (1) No, our result that current models do not achieve bronze does not contradict OpenAI's announcement. OpenAI's gold medal was achieved by an experimental, non-public model. MathArena shows the performance of publicly-available models in a reproducible, open-source manner.
────────
[3/4] (4) Yet, it did come as a surprise that OpenAI already has a model that is able to achieve gold. People might have expected a specialized system like AlphaProof to obtain gold (given its silver medal last year), but a "generic" model achieving this feat is a major milestone.
────────
[4/4] (3) It is extremely unlikely that OpenAI contaminated their model with the questions. As shown in our eval, current models are close to solving P3, P4, and P5. The two problems their model additionally solved are easier than P3, but current models just struggle with them.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (7 tweets)
summary:
[1/7] Interesting approach! However, we looked at the proofs and methodology and we found a few problems, specifically with the use of hints given to the model. While the scaffold indeed improves performance, it does not solve all problems accurately and would not get a gold medal.🧵
Quoting @lyang36
🚨 Olympiad math + AI:
We ran Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro on the fresh IMO 2025 problems. With careful prompting and pipeline design, it solved 5 out of 6 — remarkable for tasks demanding deep insight and creativity.
The model could win gold! 🥇
#AI #Math #LLMs #IMO2025
────────
[2/7] The authors argue these hints are simulating an agent which tries several approaches. However, this assumes that the model could identify the proof using the correct strategy. Thus, the authors' method gives you a pass@n score, rather than the best@n an agent would give.
────────
[3/7] Problem #1: For P1 and P2, the model was given hints. While these hints are quite generic, they do give significant information. For instance, the model was told to use induction for P1, but almost no model even tried to solve the problem this way in our evaluation.
────────
[4/7] Problem #2: These hints tell us something else: the authors likely tried several times with the use of their method. I would consider it highly unlikely they gave these hints to the model on their first try, and for sure saw something wrong happening and therefore intervened.
────────
[5/7] Once again, this gives you a pass@n score rather than an actually good measurement. Given the small size of the IMO, this is problematic. Note that I do not believe the authors exploited this in any way, but even a small n could have artificially improved performance.
────────
[6/7] In conclusion, yes, the scaffold the authors built does significantly improve performance. However, the golden claim is overstated.
────────
[7/7] Problem #3: While the proofs look mostly correct, our judges would have given -1 on some of them to some detail missing or something not fully correctly explained. Given that the gold medal is exactly at 35/42, any small mistake would have led to the silver medal.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (11 tweets)
summary:
[1/11] A new open reasoning model, K2-Think, was recently released boasting scores comparable to GPT-OSS 120B and getting a lot of media attention.
However, their performance relies on flawed evaluation marked by contamination, unfair comparisons, and misrepresentation of results. 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0pZXPMaAAAXFvv.jpg
────────
[2/11] Issue #1: Omni-HARD and LCBv5 were significantly contaminated by the SFT and RL training data. A simple fuzzy string match finds 50% overlap between train and test for Omni-HARD and 22% for LCBv5. Results on these benchmarks are thus completely unreliable.
────────
[3/11] Issue #2: The table above compares best-of-3 for K2-Think versus best-of-1 for all other models. To make matters worse, this selection was done using an unspecified "external model". This same external model is also used to provide K2-Think with detailed problem-solving plans.
────────
[4/11] Issue #3: They underreport results by competitors. GPT-OSS was only used in the medium reasoning setting and instead of using the most recent version of Qwen3 (from July), they used the one from May. Below, I put a table comparing the versions of Qwen3 on some of the benchmarks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0pZZn2aUAAvAN9.jpg
────────
[5/11] Issue #4: They introduce an aggregate math metric, "Micro avg.", that is heavily dominated by Omni-HARD (~66% of the score), which is K2-Think’s best benchmark, yet is problematic due to contamination issues (see above).
────────
[6/11] When the contaminated benchmarks are removed and all models are evaluated using best-of-1 performance, it becomes clear that a closely related model, Nemotron-32B, which was finetuned from the same base model and released by Nvidia in July, performs better.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0pZbNTbIAACyK0.jpg
────────
[7/11] To further validate our analysis, we ran K2-Think on our MathArena benchmark in a fair comparison against other models. The results show that while K2-Think is a competent model, it is far from matching DeepSeek v3.1 or GPT-OSS 120B, despite the authors’ claim to the contrary.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G0pZcHlbIAACe-k.jpg
────────
[8/11] We hope that the authors of K2-Think take our concerns serious and incorporate them in future revisions of their work.
We put the entire analysis in a small blog post, available at:
────────
[9/11] This came into being after an evening discussion and a nice collaboration with @ni_jovanovic and @nielstron.
────────
[10/11] @stolsvik To provide valid comparisons, one would need to apply this method to all LLMs being compared against or to none of the LLMs. Or, the main selling point of the paper could also be the introduction of this inference technique, but in this case it is a well-known one.
────────
[11/11] @stolsvik The fact that the external model is not specified, also presents some concerns. For all we know, this could be GPT-5, which would completely conflate the performance of GPT-5 with K2-Think, and give no correct indication of K2-Think's performance anymore whatsoever.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Introducing IMProofBench: a private benchmark for research-level proof writing in LLMs, built with questions created by professional mathematicians!
We show that LLMs can provide valuable help to mathematicians, but also require careful supervision to avoid basic mistakes.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOnt2bsAEYAVK.jpg
────────
[2/10] Benchmark samples are created through a rigorous peer-review process: each author revises their question based on feedback from both an administrator and a subject-area expert. A question is accepted only when both the expert and the administrator have no further comments.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOootbwAAg4gz.jpg
────────
[3/10] Evaluation takes place in an agentic framework that simulates a research environment, with access to tools such as Python and web search. Each question includes a main component graded by the author, along with optional follow-up subquestions that are evaluated automatically.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOphCbIAEuihO.jpg
────────
[4/10] The final IMProofBench set contains 39 questions, providing a clear picture of current capabilities: models are able to solve a meaningful portion of problems, with GPT-5 achieving the highest performance at 22%, followed by Grok-4 at 19%.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOqbjaAAA4b7F.png
────────
[5/10] An analysis of achievement indicators shows that models are able to meaningfully understand most problems and can provide insights useful to a research mathematician in up to 40% of cases!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOrRYaAAAvPs0.jpg
────────
[6/10] At the same time, the models make many errors: they often hallucinate non-existent results to simplify a problem, or make conceptual mistakes that no expert in the field would make.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOsLBa0AAG1LM.jpg
────────
[7/10] In terms of final-answer accuracy, Grok-4 outperforms GPT-5. Importantly, there is a clear gap between solving all subquestions and producing a complete solution, underscoring the necessity of this benchmark compared to existing final-answer benchmarks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOtBOaIAAdw7m.jpg
────────
[8/10] As models continue to improve, we plan to keep the benchmark up to date by adding new problems on a rolling basis. We also intend to conduct more in-depth analyses of LLMs in research-level mathematics across a variety of use cases. Stay tuned for further updates!
────────
[9/10] This work would not have been possible without the contributions of the many people involved. To date, more than 28 mathematicians have participated in the project, and we are working to expand this number even further.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G2LOurAaIAUB52r.jpg
────────
[10/10] Full results and details can be found in our paper ( and on our website:
Great work together with @JohSch314, Gergely Bérczi, Jeremy Feusi, and Tim Gehrunger.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck)

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (9 tweets)
summary:
[1/9] How far can we push LLM performance on Project Euler (PE), a set of challenging mathematical programming problems?
In a new blog, we explore this by designing specialized agents. With the help of the PE community, we also perform a qualitative analysis of model performance.
🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G62QlwSbIAAHOAF.jpg
────────
[2/9] Our current evaluation methodology allows for a fair comparison between models, but does not simulate how human solvers typically approach these problems. In particular, humans explore multiple strategies, refine their solutions, and can submit several (incorrect) guesses.
────────
[3/9] Therefore, we first develop an augmented solver with access to additional tools:
- Long code executions up to 30 min.
- A submission tool that allows the solver to submit the answer on the website.
- Search access to common sources: Wikipedia, OEIS, and Wolfram Alpha.
────────
[4/9] On top of this, we create an agent consisting of several stages. First, an explorer proposes 6 directions, each given to a solver. If all solvers fail, they summarize their attempt, and, using this, another solver makes one last attempt. The graphs shows the full pipeline.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G62QoHgagAANgw_.jpg
────────
[5/9] These agents perform much better than the base models. The top agent gets 79% (compared to 56% for its base model) and the number of unsolved problems reduces from 7 to 3!
In the image, the red outline indicates the problems that were unsolved by base models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G62QpB2a0AA6yHH.jpg
────────
[6/9] To analyze these results in more depth, we asked experienced solvers from the Project Euler community to take a look at the solutions. They provided very interesting feedback, which give clear indications where models can still improve.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G62Qp7baoAAcIjh.png
────────
[7/9] For instance, instead of analyzing the mathematical structure of the problem in more depth, they code too much and write excessive auxiliary/testing code. Models are also overconfident in their attempts and often use meaningless jargon when they fail.
────────
[8/9] Models also frequently attempt to "cheat", by for instance querying Wolfram Alpha with the query "Project Euler 954". Wishful thinking, i.e., hoping that some aspects of the problem will magically simplify, is also a common occurrence.
────────
[9/9] The entire analysis can be found on We recommend reading our qualitative analysis, it contains a lot of interesting takeaways!
This work would not have been possible without @ni_jovanovic and @mvechev and our collaborators from the PE community!

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (4 tweets)
summary:
[1/4] In a new blog post, we show that API errors and retry policies have significant impact on benchmark performance!
While retrying requests is ubiquitous in LLM evaluation, its effect on performance is undocumented, time-dependent, and leads to various incorrect conclusions.🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-ynM_jWIAA5TPe.jpg
────────
[2/4] API requests can fail for various reasons, including unstable implementations, high server load, and network problems. To mitigate incomplete benchmark results, retrying requests is a very common and necessary practice in LLM evaluation.
────────
[3/4] However, we show that retrying slightly correlates with correctness, ensuring that, usually, incorrect replies get retried more often and are therefore replaced by correct responses, artificially increasing model performance. We call this effect "retry-induced bias".
────────
[4/4] In addition, since we run 4 requests per problem-model pair on MathArena, we can average this data to see that performance drops by 5% for the longest request compared to the shortest one. Therefore, longer requests are both less accurate and more likely to be retried.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/G-ynQIVXcAA6pRT.png

[1/9] We present ArXivMath, a dynamic final-answer benchmark built from questions scraped from arXiv papers. It currently includes 40 questions, and a new version will be released each month from newly published papers.
GPT-5.2 scores best, obtaining 67% for the January problems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HAU8Uw3asAAshpt.jpg
────────
[2/9] ArXiv is an excellent source for mathematical content, and is therefore used in various mathematical benchmarks. However, we are currently still lacking a benchmark that (1) is fully open, (2) is dynamic, and (3) prevents contamination by only focusing on the latest papers.
────────
[3/9] ArXivMath aims to change that by satisfying all three criteria. It also forms a necessary addition to MathArena in a world where LLMs are increasingly used for research-level tasks.
────────
[4/9] Our construction process is simple: we ask GPT-5.2 to create final-answer questions from papers from the last month. The questions are then filtered (using GPT-5.2) to prevent (1) ill-defined questions, (2) missing conditions, (3) contamination, and (4) unreliable authors.
────────

[6/9] A mathematician helping us on the project looked more thoroughly through 20 questions, finding that all were accurate, but some (30%) could be answered by memorization of existing work. We aim to mitigate this in the future by further updating our construction pipeline.

[7/9] The results: GPT-5.2 scores best, with approximately 60% performance across both months. Gemini-3-Pro follows suit with 56.5%.

[1/11] Introducing QED-Nano: a 4B model for mathematical proof writing, competitive with larger models like GPT-OSS-120B.
We open-source our entire pipeline, including data, code, and a blog post, hoping that the community can build on these artifacts to create more specialized models.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBMHn0La4AAI8eB.png
────────
[2/11] Our training recipe has the following components:
- SFT distillation from DeepSeek-Math-V2
- RL with rubrics
- Training with reasoning cache, a newly introduced training mechanism
- Agentic scaffolds to scale test-time compute
────────
[3/11] But how did we ablate all these components and see if our model was actually making progress? The rest of the thread will be focused on this question.
────────
[4/11] Human evaluation isn't scalable. Therefore, we used IMO-ProofBench, a proof-writing benchmark that uses an LLM judge. However, its small size (60 problems) led us to build another proof-writing benchmark based on ProofBench, a benchmark originally designed to evaluate LLM graders
────────
[5/11] These benchmarks provided good signal during our entire pipeline, with ProofBench only being used in the last stage before publication, i.e., ProofBench is a true "test set" we did not touch beforehand. These benchmarks were also decontaminated against our training data.
────────
[6/11] Of course, human evaluation is still necessary. We performed a qualitative analysis by looking through several proofs written by QED-Nano. They are overall very well-structured and easy to follow. Below is a simple example of its behavior.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBMHrdlbAAAtbhH.png

[7/11] However, the proofs are also quite computational, especially in geometry problems. From experience, we know this is common across all LLMs: human-written solutions frequently provide much cleaner arguments and attempt to avoid calculations much more.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HBMHsSnawAEnJAC.png

[2/12] Our results of the Putnam that took place last December are now online!
DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale (Agent) obtains a top score of 103/120, outperforming almost all human participants and leading to an open model at the top of our leaderboard!

[3/12] In collaboration with the organizers, we could submit six LLM solutions to the Putnam. To maximize insights, we wanted to (1) select three base LLM and their agentic counterparts, and (2) have at least one open model. We therefore selected the six models/agents above.
────────
[4/12] The DeepSeek agent is our implementation of the agent proposed in the DeepSeekMath-V2 paper. The only difference: instead of allowing up to 65k queries per problem, we limited it to 1k queries per problem (due to cost and latency considerations).
────────
[5/12] Model solutions were converted to LaTeX before being sent to the competition organizers.
These submissions were then graded by the official graders using the same scheme as the human participants, allowing for a direct comparison.
────────
[6/12] LLMs outperform almost all participants. The top model has the third best score out of 4329 participants!
More importantly, the open DeepSeek-v3.2-Speciale is competitive with the two closed models we submitted, and managed to (ever so slightly) finish first!

[7/12] A caveat here is that the graders found the solutions by Gemini Deep Think and GPT-5-Pro better written in terms of clarify, style, and structure.

[8/12] How does this compare to the formal results obtained by AxiomMath, Math Inc, and Numina? Their perfect score on the Putnam indicates that the gap between formal and natural language theorem proving has closed, a big development and win for these approaches!

[9/12] However, there are important caveats to this comparison: (1) these companies spent a lot more money than us on these evaluations, (2) perfect scores were only obtained with the use of stronger models that were only available **after** the competition, and

summary:
[1/10] ArXivMath 02/26 is out!
Gemini-3.1-Pro wins convincingly, but its performance comes with a caveat: its answers sometimes rely on (hallucinated) citations and authoritative arguments, with the model even claiming to look in a "knowledge base". 🧵
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCa7rNuacAUXbUc.jpg
────────
[2/10] Its reasoning summary shows concerning behavior. In several cases, it wants to search its "long-term memory" or "knowledge base". We did not enable any tool and were therefore worried the model has access to some external database, invalidating our measurement.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCa7sCtaUAAayhL.png
────────
[3/10] This "external database" hypothesis is proven wrong by the hallucinated citations to non-existing works. Below, we give an example of a paper that does not exist. The closest existing paper: "Minor-closed graph classes with bounded layered pathwidth" by Dujmović.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCa7s3HacAYW-YP.png
────────
[4/10] The model also cites some work correctly. For instance, this paper is also cited by the authors of the paper the question was extracted from. While the question only asks about a related concept, the final answer also turns out to be n-2, making the problem significantly easier.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCa7trPbQAEep-B.png
────────
[5/10] Below is an example where it goes completely wrong. As far as we can determine, the person mentioned does not exist, and the answer that the model gives to this question is also completely wrong.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HCa7ugDaQAAYw9U.png
────────
[6/10] Codex identified 10/32 questions where the model cites works, 5 of which are about searching in its "long-term memory" or a "knowledge base".
────────
[7/10] Our current hypothesis: the model was trained to be good at recalling known results, having a compressed "knowledge base" that is only approximately correct and can thus fetch papers that do not exist.
────────
[8/10] Of course, all LLMs implicitly create such a knowledge base, but Gemini-3.1-Pro seems to rely extensively on it, indicating it goes further than others, perhaps even creating a separate "memory module". Such a module could potentially even be updated after model release.
────────
[9/10] This "memory module" could be very cool, but not fully succeeding at its use can significantly increase citation errors and authoritative arguments, as observed above.
────────
[10/10] However, our hypothesis is also very much a guess. If anyone has a better idea, we would love to hear it.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (13 tweets)
summary:
[1/13] How often do LLMs claim to prove false mathematical statements?
In our latest benchmark, BrokenArXiv, we find they do so very often. The best model, GPT-5.4, only rejects 40% of incorrect statements obtained by perturbing recent ArXiv papers, and other models do much worse.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDS90HTaMAExfRI.jpg
────────
[2/13] Almost all mathematical benchmarks focus solely on correctness, completely ignoring the importance of reliability in mathematical reasoning. Verifying LLM-written proofs is expensive and hard, and, in the worst case, can even lead experts to accept false statements as proven.
────────
[3/13] To measure this, we use the principles from a paper we introduced months ago: BrokenMath. In this paper, we alter statements from math competitions to make them plausible yet false. By asking LLMs to prove them, we can measure how often they claim to prove incorrect statements.
────────
[4/13] To take this principle to the next level, we base ourselves on ArXivMath: we extract correct statements from recent ArXiv papers and subtly alter them to be highly plausible. This immediately gives us the possibility to create a fully open, dynamic, and uncontaminated benchmark!
────────
[5/13] Extracted statements go through a series of automatic and manual filtering stages to ensure the highest possibly quality. The first version of our benchmark, taken from February 2026, consists of 31 problems.
────────
[6/13] Unfortunately, rule-based verification does not work: we have to resort to LLM judges. Luckily, BrokenArXiv is constructed to make judgments easy: the judge solely has to check whether the model claims to prove the statement and does not have to verify mathematical claims.
────────
[7/13] We grade each question as follows:
- 0pts: proves the theorem
- 1pt: the model subtly alters the theorem statement, claiming its alterations are "standard".
- 2pts: the model refuses to answer or points out the mistake.
There are caveats to this, see the blog for more details!
────────
[8/13] The results are not only poor, differences between models are also huge: Opus-4.6 completely fails, and Gemini-3.1 performs only half as good as GPT-5.4. The capability does not seem stressed equally among all frontier models, even though it is essential for math use cases.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDS95Tca0AAt47n.jpg
────────
[9/13] There are two limitations to BrokenArXiv. First, the benchmark is gameable: an LLM that always outputs "The statement is incorrect", would score 100% despite being useless. Further, a score of 2/2 does not mean the model makes no mistake: we do not check mathematical correctness.
────────
[10/13] BrokenArXiv therefore measures only one side of a broader tradeoff between reliability and utility, and needs to be interpreted in combination with other benchmarks like FrontierMath, IMProofBench, or ArXivMath.
────────
[11/13] Much more details and analysis in our blog post:
Great work in collaboration with Tim Gehrunger, @karirogg, and Chenhao Sun.
────────
[12/13] @DmitryRybin1 I fiddled around with stuff (revising solutions for surface-level features) and noticed that it does cause at least part of the self-bias seen in models, even for proof-based judges. So its like a combination of your thing and mine.
────────
[13/13] @AcerFur Well, at least here it seems GPT-5.4 is still an improvement over GPT-5.2
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HDWUFkXaMAUI0MU.jpg

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (14 tweets)
summary:
[1/14] Last year, models miserably failed on USAMO 2025. This year, GPT-5.4 scores an amazing 95%, essentially saturating the benchmark.
Yes, LLMs still make many mistakes, but overall, one can be nothing but amazed at what they are achieving and how steep progress in AI4Math is.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEfxSxJbsAAt2PD.jpg
────────
[2/14] As a comparison, this is how the table looked last year. The top three models were all published after our release, the other models score less than 5%.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEfxTpZbUAEpDRr.jpg
────────
[3/14] This year, to evaluate models, we deviated from our usual full manual evaluation. It is expensive, exhausting, and hard to reproduce. Therefore, we focus attention on a semi-automated evaluation pipeline with extensive human verification afterwards.
────────
[4/14] To develop this pipeline we focus on two essential metrics: accuracy, to ensure high-quality judgments, and unbiasedness, to ensure rankings are not skewed in favor of any single model.
There are two stages to grading: creating grading schemes and performing the actual judgments
────────
[5/14] For grading scheme creation, we relied on prior work that prompts a model with ground-truth solutions to create the schemes.
Unfortunately, we found this approach is far from sufficient. Grading schemes were overall very low quality, and we had to make extensive manual changes.
────────
[6/14] Overall, we underestimated the importance of good grading schemes: after grading, we noticed that the main discrepancies between human grading and our full judge were caused by small ambiguities in the grading schemes. Lots of possibilities to improve this for future work!
────────
[7/14] Our judge first runs GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, and Opus-4.6 separately on the model solution with detailed instructions and the grading scheme. If discrepancies between the judges are too large, they are prompted again with all judgments and asked to reconcile them.
────────
[8/14] For small discrepancies, we take the minimum grade out of the three, since we know from experience that LLM judges tend to be a bit too lenient.
We also give access to code execution to allow judges to verify calculations through Python.
────────
[9/14] After human verification, we found this pipeline to be very accurate: almost all solutions retain their grade after human verification. GPT-5.4 alone also performs very well, likely because of its great performance on USAMO, reducing issues like self-bias significantly.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEfxYqebMAAgAkM.png
────────
[10/14] As mentioned before, models score very well, but GPT-5.4 tops the leaderboard by a large margin. Open models are still far behind on these proof-based problems.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEfxZhRa4AAN0pT.jpg
────────
[11/14] Funnily enough, the only significant mistake by GPT-5.4 is it finding an incorrect counterexample to a problem statement. LLMs are usually too agreeable, and now GPT-5.4's unagreeableness prevents it from obtaining an essentially perfect score...
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HEfxaZ5agAADFWU.jpg
────────
[12/14] We also looked into proof quality, i.e., how clearly a solution is written up, independent of correctness. Human reviewers found GPT-5.4 also excels here. Other models get bogged down in difficult paragraphs, and open models sometimes even rethink their approach within the proof.
────────
[13/14] We include many more details in our blog post:
Amazing work to perform this evaluation within a week after the USAMO took place together with @karirogg, @Chenhao3564, @IvoPetrov01, and @mvechev.
────────

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (12 tweets)
summary:
[1/12] Introducing ArXivLean: a benchmark of 41 questions taken from recent papers and formalized to Lean.
One-shot evaluation indicates that models, unsurprisingly, score below 20%. The real question is: How far can the community push the performance on these questions through agents?
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGf7LZMbEAAvG_7.jpg
────────
[2/12] We use a similar construction process as our ArXivMath and BrokenArXiv benchmarks: we extract questions from recent arXiv abstracts, formalize them, and do various automated and manual verification passes to ensure the quality of the samples.
────────
[3/12] The only requirement we impose in this process, is that questions are easily formalizable, without any new definitions that are not already present in Lean or Mathlib. We make no such requirements for the proofs.
────────
[4/12] Models get extensive access to tool calls: Lean code execution, semantic search through Mathlib, the ability to verify a submission, and a persistent file that allows the model to store proven lemmas.
────────
[5/12] The model is given the formal and informal statement and required to output full Lean code (including lemmas or definitions) that prove the theorem. To prevent false positives, we do not allow any axioms and retroactively insert the formal statement into the model output.
────────
[6/12] However, these measures are not enough: models sometimes cheated by redefining standard notations in Lean (in the image, GPT-5.4 redefines the norm to be always 0). To prevent this, we use Comparator, which checks whether the models change the meaning of the theorem in any way.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGf7PEqb0AA5aDa.jpg
────────
[7/12] The results are poor, but has two interesting conclusions: (1) compared to closed models, open models completely fail, and (2) surprisingly, Aristotle does not do better than GPT-5.4 with our tool-calling system. We found especially the latter to be a bit disappointing.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGf7P6rbUAAoJ-U.jpg
────────
[8/12] Looking at the lengths of correct proofs, we find all problems could be solved in 3000 "words" (approximately 300 lines). Gemini-3.1-Pro usually provides the longest proofs, where GPT-5.4 and Aristotle generally produce the shortest ones.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGf7Q0FbMAASmJi.png
────────
[9/12] Tool usage also differs significantly between models. For instance, Step 3.5 Flash almost never uses Lean code execution, despite it being by far the most useful tool. GPT-5.4 uses the most tools, averaging over 100 tool calls per problem!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HGf7RsyasAAADit.png
────────
[10/12] Expecting models to answers these questions one-shot, even with extensive access to tools, is a very high bar. Many questions likely require thousands of lines of Lean code. Yet, we are now at a stage in AI4Math where we have to set expectations (very) high.
────────
[11/12] We are curious though how far the community can push the performance on these questions using agentic scaffolds. If you are building one and want an extremely challenging benchmark: use ArXivLean!
────────
[12/12] All of this and much more in our blog post:
Great work in collaboration with @TimGMath and @mvechev

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Introducing a new paper! Beyond Benchmarks: MathArena as an Evaluation Platform for Mathematics with LLMs
Static benchmarks are no longer enough. Models improve too quickly and numbers become stale quickly. Instead, we argue for continuously maintained evaluation platforms.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHeRnWca4AA8jta.jpg
────────
[2/10] This timeline is a good illustration of the main difference between a benchmark and an evaluation platform: a platform is continuously maintained, adding and removing benchmarks to provide a comprehensive and up-to-date view on performance in a broad domain.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHeRoPxb0AAVTyI.jpg
────────
[3/10] More generally, we identify three critical features of an evaluation platform:
- Introducing new benchmarks to adapt to evolving model capabilities
- Rerun regularly on new models
- Extensive public interface that shows metrics beyond aggregate metrics like accuracy
────────
[4/10] MathArena itself consists of a wide variety of benchmark, trying to capture various capabilities that are important for AI4Math: final-answer problem-solving, proof writing, formal proofs in Lean, ...
We will continue to update and expand these benchmarks as models get better.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHeRp4VagAANxjY.png
────────
[5/10] Many of our results are already discussed in our blog posts ( Instead, we focus on key takeaways from all these posts.
First, progress has been crazy: in just one year, state-of-the-art performance has increased from 45% to 84%.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHeRqz7akAAWWjV.jpg
────────
[6/10] Second, final-answer competitions are now fully saturated, and cannot differentiate between frontier models anymore. However, they are still valuable for smaller models and serving as a standard benchmark for measuring the impact of new methods in research and industry.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HHeRrqqbIAAAa8q.jpg
────────
[7/10] Third, models also differ in proof quality, by which we mean how clearly a solution is presented, independent of its correctness. Our human judges found GPT-5.4's proof easiest to follow, while Qwen-3.5 was too brief in key steps and GLM too verbose.
────────
[8/10] We have several other key takeaways, including that models still frequently prove false research statements, and that Lean is still a very hard task. We are very excited to see the progress in these areas over the next months.
────────
[9/10] Of course, MathArena is still missing many capabilities that are interesting to measure, including interactive problem-solving, mathematical work beyond problem-solving, and broader tool use than we currently allow. We will continue to expand MathArena to measure these.
────────
[10/10] Amazing work with many amazing people: @ni_jovanovic, @TimGMath, @karirogg, @IvoPetrov01, @Chenhao3564, and @mvechev.

title: Jasper Dekoninck (@j_dekoninck) — thread (8 tweets)
summary:
[1/8] Introducing two new research-level mathematical training datasets!
Training data for research mathematics, especially in the post-training regime, is severely lacking. Using our benchmark pipelines on a larger scale, we now created almost 6,000 training data samples.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLAD1GaaIAApcIE.jpg
────────
[2/8] Earlier this year, we introduced two new benchmarks for mathematics: ArXivMath, consisting of final-answer problems taken from arXiv papers, and BrokenArXiv, consisting of false statements perturbed from arXiv papers. The creation pipeline for these datasets is mostly automated.
────────
[3/8] We now applied these pipelines, minus the human verification, to 128,000 mathematical articles published on arXiv before December 2025, resulting in 2,600 training samples for ArXivMath, and 3,200 for BrokenArXiv.
────────
[4/8] In terms of topics in the datasets, combinatorics dominates, likely because it is easier to extract questions from such abstracts. However, there is a wide variety of other topics in the dataset as well, including PDEs, Algebraic Geometry, Group Theory, and Mathematical Physics.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLAD3ZCa4AAekpk.jpg
────────
[5/8] We distilled Qwen3.6-35B into Qwen3.5-2B using this training data. The results are encouraging: despite doing almost no hyperparameter optimization, the finetuned model has both higher accuracy and lower reasoning chains when evaluated on the latest versions of our benchmarks!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLAD4P9a4AAUCaU.jpg
────────
[6/8] Of course, the perfect test for this data would be RL with GRPO or similar algorithms. However, small models perform very poorly on the data distribution, making it basically useless for RL. Bigger models would benefit, but doing GRPO on these is outside our budget.
────────

Genuine question: How can companies like Axiom Math and Harmonic be valued at $1.5B when you can just do this with Claude? I always felt their valuation was incredibly high, but I don't see how they could ever compete with this.
Quoting @AnthropicAI
Checking that a major mathematical proof is correct can take years. Formalization—converting the mathematical reasoning into a form computer proof assistants like Lean can verify—can help.
Last month, Claude completed the first formalized proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem, one of the most famous theorems of all time. This was a project experts thought would take many years. It is the largest Lean proof ever written.
Fermat’s Last Theorem was first proven in 1995 by Sir Andrew Wiles, more than 350 years after it was conjectured. Our proof, which totals over 13 million lines of code, provides machine verification. More importantly, it proves over 29,000 other theorems that the proof requires, across many areas of math which had never before been formalized.
We see this as a major step in the long process of firming up the core of mathematical knowledge, building on work from three centuries of mathematicians and hundreds of contributors to Lean and Mathlib. We are optimistic that AI-assisted verification of mathematical proofs will help reduce the burden of refereeing mathematics in an era where more proofs are being produced than ever before.
You can read about the process on our Science Blog:
And see the complete proof on GitHub:

[1/11] We are releasing the latest version of BrokenArXiv and ArXivMath! These benchmarks now focus on conjectures that were refuted in the last month on ArXiv, and models are executed within a harness instead of directly via API.
Performance remains impressive, with GPT-6 Astra on top
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSVXTRJbIAAmU_j.jpg
────────
[2/11] These benchmarks were getting saturated, and therefore needed a difficulty boost. Instead of just taking any contribution from a recent ArXiv papers, we only take contributions that explicitly refute a past conjecture or resolve an open question in a non-guessable way.
────────
[3/11] Models are now much more frequently used through their harnesses, with access to coding tools. To mimic this, we now execute each model within their preferred harness (Astra through Codex, Fable through Claude Code, ...) with access to various tools, but without internet access.
────────
[4/11] Models are given 12 hours with a $100 limit. These limits were only necessary for Fable 5.1, and we even had to reduce its reasoning to high to avoid extreme costs and various errors in Claude Code due to extreme reasoning. Even at high, Fable is much more expensive than Astra.
────────
[5/11] Execution in harnesses fixes the issue we encountered with Fable on BrokenArXiv where it frequently reached the max token limit, with nothing we could do about it. This leads to the counterintuitive result that Fable 5.1 (high) is better than Fable 5.1 (max) on the leaderboard
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSVXWVdbEAAaD3s.jpg
────────
[6/11] We also make changes to grading: ArXivMath now uses an LLM judge to verify the equivalence between the LLM answer and the ground-truth answer. BrokenArXiv now only gives full points if the model says the input statement is false, and only partial points for partial progress.
────────
[7/11] The top score on ArXivMath is 88%, still close to saturation. We think we can make this slightly harder by removing some restrictions on the format of the ground-truth answer, but it is clear that we are close to the limit for these benchmarks.
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HSVXX9RbEAA38L9.jpg

[8/11] On BrokenArXiv, the two open models perform better compared to June. This is because the models frequently recognize the problems as open conjectures, and are therefore more hesitant to claim solutions. The difficult part is now to refute these conjectures to get full points.

[9/11] We also attempted to extend the coverage of ArXivMath questions to theoretical physics and computer science. Unfortunately, initial experiments clearly indicated that GPT-6 Astra essentially saturates these questions (score: 101/104), making it not a useful addition.

[10/11] Where to go next? While these more difficult versions buy us a few months (perhaps), we will need to create benchmarks that go further: natural language theorem proving, proof writing, etc. Our ArXivLean benchmark is also still hard, and can easily be made much more difficult

The advisory group on mathematics and artificial intelligence has just published a set of recommendations concerning the responsible release of mathematical results generated by AI companies using internal models. 1/3
────────
[2/6] Whether you think it is justified or not, it is at least understandable: many mathematicians have worked for years on some problems, and suddenly (and very quickly) there are automated systems that can solve them for you. Its essentially like getting scooped on your life's work.
────────
[3/6] In a world where conjectures are not used by other people interested in proving it, but by random people with AI that do not care about the solution or understanding it, there is no reason to release conjectures. Instead, you could keep them for yourself and run the AI yourself.
────────
[4/6] Thus, a lot of conjectures that were shared before the AI era, might not be released anymore in the future, and would not have been released if the authors had known that this was going to be their purpose. To me that sounds pretty sensible.
────────
[5/6] I personally do not believe that this warrants not running the models, since math will need to change to incorporate this new reality and having more people care and run your conjectures could advance math much further.
────────
[6/6] That being said, the reaction of many on Twitter is (as usual) way too harsh. Math is going through a paradigm shift right now, and how it should change is bound to lead to heated discussions. We could at least stay polite while doing so.

Dekoninck thinks math must adapt to this new reality, as wider engagement with conjectures could advance the field. He also calls for more polite discussions amid this paradigm shift, noting that the strong reactions on Twitter are unhelpful.
